assessment.nobel_worthiness: The collateral-constraint mechanism of Kiyotaki and Moore (credit cycles) explains how small shocks are amplified and persist through asset prices and borrowing limits. It became a foundation of macro-financial modelling, was used in analyses of the 2008 crisis, and underlies much of the later literature on financial frictions, leverage and macroprudential policy. Its conceptual originality and breadth of influence are very high.
assessment.attribution: The core idea is clearly credited to Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 paper. Gertler and Gilchrist are significant contributors through the related financial-accelerator line, but that line is tied to Bernanke, who is outside this list and has already been honoured for other work. A two-person prize on the collateral-constraint mechanism is the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and has been confirmed over almost three decades by theoretical extensions and by empirical work on credit cycles, housing collateral and firm investment. Timing is fully mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to credit the financial-accelerator line (Gertler, Gilchrist) alongside Kiyotaki and Moore.
Overlap with recent prizes on banking and financial crises could make it harder to argue a distinct contribution.
Direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is more contested than the theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of demand with differentiated products (BLP) and of dynamic industry models (Ericson-Pakes) changed empirical industrial organisation. It is the standard toolkit for merger analysis, antitrust, and the evaluation of trade and environmental policy. The methodological contribution is deep, widely adopted and tied to real policy practice.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the clear originators of BLP. Pakes also led the dynamic-industry framework, with Ericson, Benkard and others contributing to it. Bresnahan, Reiss and Levin are important but belong to a somewhat different strand. The three-name selection is natural but leaves out some significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: BLP (1995) and related estimators have been in use for three decades, and applications are very numerous. The contribution is fully mature.
uncertainties: The credited list is very broad and the recognition could be framed differently, for example around Bresnahan's contributions.
A prize focused mainly on methods might be weighed against more substantive findings from other fields.
Some prior recognition of IO methods through earlier prizes could affect how the committee perceives novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: These authors built the modern theory and empirics of political economics. They show how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy, public goods and development. The work links directly to growth and institutional questions, and it set the agenda for a generation of political economists.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures (the 'Political Economics' framework and the constitutional-effects empirics). Besley is a major co-contributor, especially on state capacity and accountability. The set is reasonably coherent, although Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson were recognised in 2024 for work on institutions, so the distinctness of this strand must be argued.
assessment.maturity: The research began in the early 1990s and was confirmed by two decades of cross-country and within-country empirical evidence. Timing is fully mature.
uncertainties: Possible perception of overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity.
Debates about causal identification in the cross-country constitutional comparisons.
Whether the committee would split credit between theory (Persson, Tabellini) and state-capacity work (Besley).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The firm-heterogeneity framework in trade (Melitz 2003, building on Helpman's work with Krugman and others) shifted the field's focus from industries to firms. It changed how gains from trade, selection and reallocation are understood, and spawned a very large body of empirical and quantitative work.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator of the heterogeneous-firm trade model. Helpman has a long record of contributions, including trade with increasing returns, firm-level trade patterns and multinational organisation. Redding is a major later contributor. The Melitz-Helpman pairing is natural, although some credit for the generalisation and empirics properly belongs to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation through firm-level data and structural trade models. The contribution is mature.
uncertainties: The relationship to the 2008 prize on new trade theory and credit due to others (for example Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum).
Whether the committee prefers to recognise Helpman for his broader record rather than for this specific line.
Measured welfare gains from firm selection are sensitive to modelling assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology, together with the empirical 'China shock' studies, changed understanding of labour-market polarisation, regional adjustment and the distributional effects of trade and automation. The topic has large policy and public relevance. The empirical evidence is credible and widely discussed.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the principal authors of the trade-shock studies. The task framework is shared with Autor, Levy and Murnane, and also relates to Acemoglu and Restrepo, who is outside this list. Katz has a long co-authorship record on skill-biased change. The attribution among the strands is more diffuse here than in some other cases.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 2003 to 2016. Their lasting effect has been tested, but some questions remain open, such as the persistence of trade-shock effects and the role of automation.
uncertainties: Recent prize recognition of technology and institutions (2024) may reduce the margin for this topic.
Fairly recent work, with longer-run assessments still evolving.
Whether the prize would recognise the empirical trade-shock work or the task-based conceptual framework, which are different contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Building long-run series on top incomes and wealth from tax data changed measurement and public debate on inequality, and it set a new empirical standard through the World Inequality Database. The data contributions are significant and they motivated a wave of research. The theoretical interpretation of the findings is more contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the principal creators of the top-income series, and Zucman added work on wealth and offshore assets. Saez also appears in public economics (optimal taxation), so his credit spans several lines. The attribution is reasonably clear on measurement but less so on explanatory theory.
assessment.maturity: The data work has stood for twenty years and has been repeatedly replicated. Debates about methodology, such as how to treat capital income and retirement wealth, continue.
uncertainties: Methodological criticisms of distributional national accounts and wealth-capitalisation estimates.
Whether the committee sees measurement as a distinct scientific discovery as opposed to a contribution to public debate.
Concerns about the policy advocacy accompanying the research.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave macro-development a measurable way to link firm-level distortions to cross-country differences in aggregate productivity, and it is widely used in growth accounting and policy analysis. It has real conceptual and empirical influence on the understanding of why countries differ in income.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the principal authors of the quantitative approach. Restuccia and Rogerson developed closely related contemporaneous work, so the credit is shared and could reasonably be drawn differently. Two or three names are plausible.
assessment.maturity: Developed since 2008 to 2009 and confirmed by many country studies, though identification of what counts as a distortion remains debated. The contribution is reasonably but not fully mature.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products as distortions.
Credit conflict with Restuccia and Rogerson (the latter not listed).
Relatively recent origin compared with other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Experimental and theoretical work on fairness, reciprocity and inequity aversion explained behaviour in bargaining, public goods and contracting that standard self-interest models cannot. The Fehr-Schmidt model gave a tractable formal framework used in applied theory. Impact on behavioural and experimental economics is large.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the central figure in the experimental evidence and the Fehr-Schmidt model (1999) is jointly credited. Bolton and Ockenfels developed a rival model concurrently, and Rabin's earlier reciprocity work is also relevant, so credit is shared. Falk is an important empirical contributor but is less central to the original formulation.
assessment.maturity: Developed since the late 1990s, with substantial replication across populations. Debate persists over how well lab results transfer to field settings.
uncertainties: Competing credit claims (Bolton-Ockenfels, Rabin).
External validity of lab-based results and the replicability of some social-preference experiments.
Behavioural economics has already been recognised several times, which may affect the committee's appetite.
